# FDG8106

> AVOID overloading equality operators on mutable reference types.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 8.13.2 Equality Operators on Reference Types.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG8106
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test warning
- Status: verified

Message: Avoid overloading equality operators on the mutable reference type '{0}'

FDG8106 reports the first operator == declared in a class when the class or one of its base classes declared in source has an instance field that is neither readonly nor const (the field of an auto-property with a set accessor counts; an init accessor does not, and neither does the field of an event), the same mutability test as FDG8070. Any such field counts, private ones included: a private field that is not readonly, such as a cached hash code, makes the type count as mutable. Immutable types are not reported, as the body allows. State that is mutable through a readonly field of a mutable type is not seen, so coverage is partial. CA1046 is mapped to FDG8100 instead: it reports immutable types too and leaves out types that override Equals. Removing the operators changes the public API, so the fix is breaking; there is no code fix.

## From the book

Many languages have built-in equality operators for reference types. The built-in operators usually implement the reference equality, and many developers are surprised when the default behavior is changed to the value equality.

This problem is mitigated for immutable reference types because immutability makes it much harder to notice the difference between reference equality and value equality.
